transcript:
Header: 2025-10-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 min | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO - TidalMesh), Priya Kapoor (Platform Eng Manager), Evan Ruiz (Security)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Quick agenda — packaging, KMS, perf, telemetry, rollout plan. Luca will do the deep bits. Rajiv, Priya, Evan — want to start with any specific constraints?

00:22 Rajiv: Yeah thanks Maya. Major things for us — no public egress for model payloads, KMS must be HSM backed, and marketplace listing needs a tidy installer we can hand to our ops team. Timeline is end of November for pilot. We also have to prove low token latency for chat workloads.

00:40 Luca: Got it. We built two packaging options — a Helm chart with opinionated defaults, and an operator for more hands-off lifecycle. Helm is faster for trial; operator is better for enterprise upgrades. For the marketplace listing we typically publish the helm chart plus a containerized connector and a short ref‑arch doc.

01:05 Priya: Helm sounds fine for pilot but how much customization is needed? Our cluster needs custom CNI and we have strict network egress rules.

01:18 Luca: Helm values let you inject your CNI annotations and set egress to cluster‑local. We can include an example values file for TidalMesh in the repo. There might be a couple of places where you need to set the liveness/readiness probes based on your node sizes — we'll include comments.

01:33 Evan: About KMS — we use an HSM provider (Thales) and KMS lives on a separate VLAN. How does Redwood handle key wrapping and rotation? We need to show that private keys never leave customer network.

01:48 Luca: Good question. For Private deployments we offer customer‑managed KMS integration. The connector supports KMS calls over mTLS to your KMS endpoint. Keys never land in Redwood control plane. For HSMs, we support the PKCS#11 path and can accept wrapped keys. We'll need a test credential and an IP allowlist to the lab.

02:12 Rajiv: Can you run a quick diagram — how requests flow? We want assurance tokens don't traverse outside.

02:21 Maya: Sure, quick high level — user request -> TidalMesh frontend -> on‑prem gateway/connector -> local model pool (or cache) -> response. For exceptions we can route to Redwood hosted fallback but that can be disabled for air‑gapped.

02:40 Luca: I'll share a quick slide later. Note on fallback — we can configure automatic fallback to a smaller hosted model only if allowed, otherwise it stays local. That’s often a compliance toggle.

03:00 Priya: Perf — we saw notes in the README about quantization profiles. What's the SLA we can expect for 512 token chat sequences on an A100 equivalent?

03:14 Luca: Real numbers vary. From our lab runs: 512 tokens with q4_0 quantization on an A100-ish node gives median ~120ms per token generation in a streaming scenario, but that depends on batching and KV cache efficacy. If you need lower p99 latency we set tighter batching windows and reduce batch sizes; that increases cost.

03:38 Rajiv: Wait, q4_0? We typically compress to int8. Are you recommending q4_0 over int8 for NVidia gear?

03:47 Luca: q4_0 trades off some accuracy but is much faster for attention ops on typical inference kernels. Int8 can be better in some custom kernels but tends to increase memory and sometimes latency due to dequant paths. We'll run a targeted microbenchmark for your model and report back.

04:05 Evan: Also need to know about telemetry — what logs are sent to Redwood and can we keep them local? Audit log retention is a must.

04:14 Maya: For Private mode telemetry is limited. We ship aggregated metrics (latency, token counts) to the control plane unless you opt‑out. Audit logs can be stored in‑customer S3 or forwarded to your SIEM. We have RBAC controls to obfuscate user content.

04:33 Priya: Helm chart — what about operator? Are there breaking changes when we switch from helm to operator later?

04:42 Luca: Operator will manage CRDs for model resources and rollouts. We design migration patch scripts; in practice it's a controlled migration. For Marketplace listing we typically recommend helm for first release, operator as v2.

05:00 Rajiv: Marketplace listing requires a short reference architecture doc and quickstart. Can Redwood provide a prefilled doc we can customize?

05:09 Maya: Yes, we'll share a TidalMesh‑specific ref‑arch and quickstart. It will include diagram, values.yaml sample, and troubleshooting. Also we'll attach the compliance checklist used for Marketplace gating.

05:25 Priya: On networking there's one more — can the connector use nodePort or does it require LoadBalancer? Our on‑prem infra doesn't support cloud load balancers.

05:36 Luca: It supports both. We provide an ingress example for MetalLB and a nodePort fallback. We'll include both patterns in the repo and call out recommended annotations.

06:00 [link dropped in chat: https://redwood.example.com/marketplace/tidalmesh-stub-repo]

06:12 Rajiv: Cool. About rollout: success criteria for us — installable with Helm, KMS handshake success, run a smoke chat workload under 200ms median latency, and audit logs landing in our S3. Can those be UAT gates?

06:29 Maya: Yes, totally. We'll codify those into a UAT checklist and share. UAT target date — you mentioned end of November — we should schedule a joint run on Nov 12.

06:45 Evan: Security review — we need your SOC2 Type II and also a data flow map for external endpoints. Also, SSO must be SAML2 backed.

06:57 Maya: I'll attach SOC2. SAML2 SSO is supported via the console for user auth. The connector supports service account tokens too for machine auth. We'll include a sample SAML metadata exchange template.

07:15 Priya: Anything we need to change in our helm repo to be marketplace ready?

07:22 Luca: Minimal — add a values.schema.json, annotate charts with provenance and set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent. Also sign the charts. We'll give a preflight script that runs linting and simple smoke tests.

07:40 Rajiv: A couple of gotchas — we saw mention of KV cache behaviour in the doc and the term K-V cache was spelled different ways in the README — minor but for clarity, we want the cache retained per conversation id.

07:55 Luca: Yes, that should be default. We'll add a config example: conversation_id -> kv_cache_key, with TTL settings. We'll also add an opt‑out for cache sharing across sessions.

08:10 Maya: Quick objection we often hear — customers ask 'why Redwood and not VectorGate or CloudFabric?' Any thoughts from your side on differentiators we should emphasize in the marketplace listing?

08:22 Luca: Emphasize unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, clear quantization recommendations, and built‑in fallback policies — and the observability hooks. We won't call out competitor names in listing, but we'll highlight the production controls.

08:40 Rajiv: On pricing — for pilot we just need a dev license. Who handles dev credits?

08:47 Maya: We'll put a 3‑month dev package on the pilot and detail estimated token cost for your expected load. I'll include a simple cost calculator sheet.

09:00 Priya: Last thing — automation. Can we embed GitOps? We want an example Argo CD app manifest.

09:08 Luca: Yes, sample ArgoCD app + flux kustomize overlay in the stub repo.

09:20 Maya: Ok great. Recap and next steps. Recap: Redwood to share packaging checklist, stub repo link, SOC2, and quickstart. Luca to run lab install and perf microbenchmarks and send results. TidalMesh to provide KMS test credentials and network egress rules. Schedule UAT for Nov 12.

09:42 Rajiv: Sounds good. Anything else from security?

09:48 Evan: We'll review the SOC2 and send any follow‑up questions. Also will want a short runbook for key rotation.

09:56 Maya: Great — I'll follow up after this with actions. Thanks everyone.

10:02 [meeting ended]

Notes: Transcription has noisy bits (PKCS 11 might appear as P-K C-S eleven in raw auto transcript). 'quantization' sometimes transcribed as 'quanta size' in a few places. Refer to the attached stub repo for exact files.
